chunks: The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me of it from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Nuʿaym al-Ṣaḥḥāf, who said:
I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The mother of my two children sees blood while she is pregnant; how should she act regarding salat (prayer)?

He said: If the pregnant woman sees blood after twenty days have passed from the time in the month when she used to see blood and remain seated, then that is not from the womb nor from menstruation. So she should perform wudu (ablution), place cotton, and perform salat (prayer). But if the pregnant woman sees blood before the time in which she used to see a small amount of blood, or at that time in that month, then it is from menstruation. So she should refrain from salat (prayer) for the number of days she used to remain seated during her menses. If the blood stops before that, then she should perform ghusl (ritual bath) and perform salat (prayer).

But if the blood does not stop except after the days in which she used to see blood have passed by one or two days, then she should perform ghusl (ritual bath), place cotton, bind herself, and perform the noon and afternoon salat (prayer). Then she should observe: if the blood, between that time and sunset, does not flow past the back of the cotton, then she should perform wudu (ablution) and perform salat (prayer) at each prayer so long as she has not removed the cotton. If she removes the cotton from herself and the blood flows, ghusl becomes obligatory upon her. But if she removes the cotton and the blood does not flow, then she should perform wudu (ablution) and perform salat (prayer), and there is no ghusl upon her.

He said: If the blood, when the cotton holds it, flows from behind the cotton in a pouring manner and does not cease, then she must perform ghusl (ritual bath) three times in every day and night, then place cotton and perform salat (prayer): she performs ghusl for fajr, and performs ghusl for ẓuhr and ʿaṣr, and performs ghusl for maghrib and the later ʿishāʾ. He said: And likewise the mustaḥāḍah acts, for when she does that, Allah removes the blood from her.

key_terms.الدَّمَ: the blood whose legal status is being determined
key_terms.الطَّمْثِ: menstruation, as distinguished from other bleeding
key_terms.الْحَامِلُ: the pregnant woman discussed in the ruling
key_terms.الْحَيْضَةِ: the menstrual period counted for suspending salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath required in certain cases of bleeding
key_terms.الْكُرْسُفِ: cotton used to absorb and monitor the bleeding
key_terms.الْمُسْتَحَاضَةُ: a woman experiencing istiḥāḍah who follows similar rulings

ai.seo_question: What should a pregnant woman do about salat (prayer) if she sees blood, and when are wudu (ablution) or ghusl required?
ai.summary: This hadith gives legal rulings on how a pregnant woman should deal with bleeding in relation to salat (prayer), distinguishing between blood treated as menstruation and blood treated as istiḥāḍah-like discharge based on timing and flow. It also explains when wudu (ablution) is sufficient and when ghusl (ritual bath) is required, and states that the mustaḥāḍah follows the same practice in the case of continuous flowing blood.
